query: Why is belt drift dangerous and what early signs should a trainee watch for?

text_chunks.title: Uneven Loading → Belt Drift → Structural Damage
text_chunks.content: Uneven Loading → Belt Drift → Structural Damage Cause: Coal from the feeder drops consistently to one side of the belt (e.g., feeder gate partially blocked, chute misaligned). The belt carries more load on one side than the other. What Happens: The belt gradually drifts toward the heavier side. It contacts the steel frame of the conveyor structure. Friction between the belt edge and the frame generates heat. Over hours, the belt edge begins to abrade. Coal spillage begins at the affected side. If not corrected, the belt tears longitudinally — a full-length split requiring complete belt replacement. Early Signs: Belt sway alarm activates. Visible drift at one or more idler sets. Spillage on one side only. Squealing noise from belt-structure contact. Consequence: Forced conveyor shutdown. Belt replacement cost (₹10–40 lakhs). 2–5 days of downtime for re-belting.

text_chunks.title: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment)
text_chunks.content: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment) The belt naturally tends to drift (wander sideways) if there is any asymmetry — uneven loading, idlers not perfectly perpendicular to belt travel, wind, or a bent frame. Even a slight drift accumulates over the length of the belt. If not corrected, the belt edge contacts the conveyor structure, causing edge damage, spillage, and ultimately belt failure. Self-aligning idlers and training idlers are used to correct drift automatically. A drifted belt that contacts the steel structure can generate enough heat through friction to ignite coal dust — causing a conveyor fire. Belt fires in CHP are a major risk and have caused plant outages lasting weeks.

text_chunks.title: Safety Device Reference Guide
text_chunks.content: Safety Device Reference Guide Device | Location on Conveyor | Function | Response When Activated ; Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) | Both sides, full length of conveyor, approximately every 30–50 m | Allows any person anywhere along the conveyor to immediately stop it in an emergency by pulling the rope/wire | Immediate emergency stop of conveyor drive motor. Conveyor cannot restart until EPC is reset and root cause investigated. ; Belt Sway Switch (BSW) | Both sides, spaced every 50–75 m along carry and return strand | Detects lateral drift of the belt beyond a set limit. Has two positions: first position = alarm; second position = trip. | First activation: Alarm in control room. Second (greater drift): Conveyor trip. Prevents belt edge from contacting steel structure. ; Zero Speed Switch (ZSS) | Tail pulley shaft or on a return idler | Monitors belt speed. Detects if the belt has stopped (zero speed) while the motor is still running — indicating belt slip. | Conveyor trip + alarm. Prevents drive pulley from running against a stationary belt (which causes fire from friction). ; Belt Weigher (BW) | Fixed location on the conveyor, typically mid-span | Measures the weight of coal on the belt per unit length using load cells. Calculates instantaneous TPH and cumulative tonnes. | Data sent to control room / DCS. No trip — provides operational data. High load may trigger an alarm. ; Chute Blocked Detector (CBD) | Inside transfer chutes at transfer points | Detects when coal has accumulated and blocked the chute (using vibration probe, ultrasonic, or paddle switch). | Alarm in control room. May automatically stop upstream feeder to prevent further coal accumulation. ; Thermal / Fire Detector | Inside conveyor galleries (tunnels) and transfer towers | Detects elevated temperature indicating a developing fire. Linear heat detection cable runs along the belt gallery roof. | Fire alarm. Conveyor trip. Activation of fire suppression system (CO₂ or water mist). Control room alert. ; Underspeed Switch | Drive shaft area | Detects if belt is running slower than designed speed (but not zero). Indicates overloading or drive slip developing. | Alarm → trip if underspeed persists. Allows early intervention before full slippage occurs. ; Motor Overload Relay (OLR) | Motor control centre (MCC) / switchgear panel | Monitors motor current. If the motor draws current above the rated limit for a set time (indicating overload), it trips. | Motor trip + alarm. Conveyor stops. Investigation required to identify overload cause before restart. When you walk a conveyor on site, you will see red ropes, yellow boxes, and small switches mounted on the frame at regular intervals — these are all part of this safety system. You will hear terms like "BSW trip," "ZSS alarm," or "EPC activation" on the radio constantly. Now you know exactly what each term means, what triggered it, and what the plant team needs to do in response. On some plants, under production pressure, well-meaning but incorrect actions include bypassing a belt sway switch that keeps tripping, disabling a chute blocked detector that gives "false" alarms, or tying off an EPC that was accidentally pulled. This is an extremely dangerous practice. Every safety device bypass removes one layer of protection from the system. Multiple bypasses create a condition where a fatal accident can occur without any warning. As an intern, if you are ever asked to bypass a safety device, immediately consult your supervisor. Document it. Never accept it as routine.

text_chunks.title: Glossary of CHP & Belt Conveyor Terms
text_chunks.content: Glossary of CHP & Belt Conveyor Terms On your first day on site you will hear these terms constantly. This glossary ensures you are not lost in the conversation. Term | Meaning ; Belt | The continuous rubber-fabric loop that carries coal from tail to head end. ; Belt Conveyor (BC) | The complete conveyor assembly — numbered in sequence (BC-1, BC-2, etc.) in the plant. ; Carry Strand | The top run of the belt that carries coal toward the discharge point. ; Return Strand | The lower run of the empty belt going back from head to tail. ; Head Pulley | The drive pulley at the discharge end of the conveyor. ; Tail Pulley | The non-driven pulley at the loading end. ; Idler | A free-spinning roller that supports the belt. Troughing idlers (carry) and flat idlers (return). ; Trough Angle | The angle at which wing idler rolls are tilted to form the trough (20°–45°). ; Take-up | The tensioning device — gravity, screw, or hydraulic — that keeps the belt at correct tension. ; Lagging | Rubber coating on the drive pulley surface to increase friction with the belt. ; Skirt Board | Side rubber/steel walls at the feed point that contain coal on the belt edge. ; Scraper / Cleaner | A blade pressed against the belt at the head end to remove carryback coal. ; Carryback | Fine coal that sticks to the belt after discharge and is carried back on the return strand. ; Transfer Point | Location where coal moves from one conveyor to the next via a chute. ; Chute | The steel guide structure that directs coal from one conveyor to the next at transfer points. ; Tripper Car | A movable discharge device on a conveyor above the bunker that distributes coal across bunker bays. Term | Meaning ; Bunker | Large coal storage silo above the boiler, fed by the conveyor. Buffer for continuous boiler feeding. ; Hopper | A funnel-shaped collection vessel below the wagon tippler that collects unloaded coal. ; Feeder | A device (vibrating, apron, or belt type) that controls the rate of coal feeding onto the conveyor. ; TPH | Tonnes Per Hour — the standard unit of conveyor throughput capacity. ; CHP | Coal Handling Plant — the entire system for receiving, processing, and conveying coal in a power plant. ; DCS | Distributed Control System — the central computerised control system monitoring all CHP parameters. ; MCC | Motor Control Centre — the electrical switchgear panel that starts, stops, and protects conveyor motors. ; EPC | Emergency Pull Cord — the safety rope running the full length of the conveyor for emergency stop. ; BSW | Belt Sway Switch — sensor that detects lateral belt drift and triggers alarm/trip. ; ZSS / USS | Zero Speed Switch / Underspeed Switch — detects belt slippage or stall. ; LOTO | Lockout-Tagout — energy isolation procedure before maintenance on conveyor or any equipment. ; Nip Point | The point where the belt meets a pulley — the most dangerous entanglement zone. ; Belt Drift | Lateral wandering of the belt off centre — can cause edge damage and fire. ; Tight Side | The belt strand leaving the drive pulley (carry side) — where belt tension is highest. ; Slack Side | The belt strand returning to the drive pulley — where tension is lower. ; CWP | Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis — lung disease caused by long-term coal dust inhalation ("black lung").

text_chunks.title: Belt Drift (Belt Misalignment)
text_chunks.content: Belt Drift (Belt Misalignment) Root Cause: Off-centre loading (feeder से coal belt के center में नहीं गिर रही), worn idlers, wet/sticky coal जो एक तरफ build-up कर रही हो, misaligned pulleys, या incorrect take-up tension। Effect: Belt एक तरफ रगड़ती है conveyor structure से → belt edge fraying → material spillage → structure damage → fire risk (friction से)। Detection: BSW (Belt Sway Switch) alarm; visual patrol में belt edge की position देखें। Immediate Action: Feed rate कम करें → self-aligning idlers adjust करें → loading pattern investigate करें। BSW trip के बाद investigation के बिना restart नहीं।

text_chunks.title: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour
text_chunks.content: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour A transfer point is like a controlled handover baton pass — coal must land precisely on the next belt. Any miss, blockage, or misalignment at this point disrupts the entire downstream flow. Wherever coal moves from one conveyor to the next — or from a hopper to a conveyor — there is a transfer point . These are not minor connections; they are among the most critical and most hazardous locations in the entire Coal Handling Plant. Understanding what happens at a transfer point is essential before entering the CHP. BC-1 (Upper Conveyor) Coal on BC-1 Head Pulley TRANSFER CHUTE (guides coal) ↓ Coal falls here BC-2 (Lower Conveyor) Impact Zone Coal on BC-2 ⚠ DUST ⚠ Spillage ⚠ Spillage ⚠ BLOCKAGE RISK Wet/sticky coal can block chute Coal must land centrally on BC-2 belt. Any deviation → spillage or belt drift.

text_chunks.title: इस Course को पूरा करने के बाद आप क्या कर पाएंगे
text_chunks.content: इस Course को पूरा करने के बाद आप क्या कर पाएंगे ये learning outcomes define करते हैं कि इस L1 course को complete करने के बाद एक intern या trainee operator को क्या demonstrate करना चाहिए। ये सिर्फ theoretical knowledge नहीं — ये observable behaviours हैं। Context & Importance: Thermal power generation cycle explain कर पाना — coal से electricity तक — और belt conveyor की critical role इस chain में। Component Recognition: एक real conveyor पर सभी major components — belt, pulleys, idlers, take-up, scrapers, chute — identify और name कर पाना। Working Principle: Friction-drive principle explain करना — tight side/slack side tension का concept — और यह conveyor reliability को कैसे affect करता है। Capacity Factors: TPH capacity को affect करने वाले factors (width, speed, trough angle, coal properties) identify करना और normal vs. abnormal loading recognize करना। Transfer Points: Transfer point पर coal flow को describe करना — chute function, impact zone, और common hazards (blockage, spillage, dust) explain करना। Hazard Recognition: Primary mechanical hazards (entanglement, nip points, struck-by), dust hazards (CWP, explosion), और fire hazards को identify करना। Safety Devices: EPC, BSW, ZSS, Belt Weigher, Chute Blocked Detector, और Thermal Detector — हर device का function और trip condition बताना। LOTO Procedure: LOTO के सभी 8 steps सही sequence में बताना और यह explain करना कि LOTO किसी भी maintenance activity से पहले क्यों mandatory है। Control Points: CP1 से CP5 तक की locations और हर point पर क्या check करना है — यह describe करना। Failure Recognition: 6 common failure cases — belt drift, overloading, chute blockage, belt slip, dust fire, entanglement — identify करना और हर case में immediate action बताना।

text_chunks.title: Common Mistakes in Assisted Execution
text_chunks.content: Common Mistakes in Assisted Execution These are the execution errors that occur most often among trainees during their first supervised interactions with feeder systems. They are not listed to make you nervous — they are listed so you recognise the pattern if you start heading toward it. Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Severity ; Touching the start button before supervisor confirms system readiness | Eagerness to help; mistaking presence of button for permission to use it | Feeder starts before downstream belt is ready; spillage or belt trip | HIGH ; Standing in the coal discharge fall zone during observation | Wanting a better viewing angle; not knowing the designated safe observation point | Coal impact injury; coal dust inhalation; being caught in moving material | HIGH ; Treating inspection as a quick visual pass — not pausing to observe carefully | Time pressure; assumption that nothing will be wrong | Hazardous material (tramp iron, oversized coal) enters the system undetected | HIGH ; Not reporting an early warning condition because "it seems minor" | Self-doubt; not wanting to raise a false alarm; not knowing what normal is | Small issues become failures; early warning missed means later incident | HIGH ; Walking away from the feeder during the post-start observation window | Feeling that once it starts, the job is done | Abnormal behaviour in the first 60 seconds goes undetected | MEDIUM ; Not accounting for inertia during a stop — assuming coal stops when the motor stops | Intuition from everyday experience (switches turn things off instantly) | Misreads the discharge end as clear when coal is still flowing; wrong report | MEDIUM ; Attempting to remove obstruction from the feeder trough | Wanting to solve the problem; not wanting to slow things down | Entanglement injury; crush injury; falls into trough | CRITICAL / FATAL

text_chunks.title: Safety & Hazard Awareness
text_chunks.content: Safety & Hazard Awareness Moving machinery + bulk material + confined spaces = continuous risk. Most conveyor accidents happen not because of complexity but because someone was not aware of where the danger was. You do not need to be doing anything wrong to be injured near a conveyor. You simply need to be in the wrong place, distracted, or unaware of what is moving around you. The conveyor does not slow down for you. It does not have a sensor that detects a human body near it. It will continue running at full speed regardless. Your awareness is your protection. MOVING BELT (entire length is a hazard) TAIL PULLEY 🔴 PINCH ZONE Entanglement risk DRIVE PULLEY 🔴 PINCH + NIP ZONE High-torque crush risk 🟠 FEED POINT Impact hazard Dust cloud 🟠 TRANSFER POINT Spillage, blockage Confined space 🟡 BELT SURFACE Never touch/step on moving belt 🟡 Return strand — carryback coal falls here — slip hazard below ☁ Dust cloud ☁ Dust cloud ━━━ Emergency Pull Cord (full length) — Pull anywhere to STOP conveyor ━━━ HAZARD ZONE LEGEND RED = Extreme danger (pinch/nip/crush) — Mandatory guarding required ORANGE = High hazard (spillage, blockage, dust, confined space) — Permit required YELLOW = Caution zone (moving belt, carryback, slipping) — Stay clear, PPE required

text_chunks.title: Safety और Hazard Awareness
text_chunks.content: Safety और Hazard Awareness Belt conveyor एक विशाल machine है जो आपसे बहुत तेज़ चलती है और बहुत ज़्यादा ताकतवर है। यह आपको नहीं देखती। आपको ही इसे देखना होगा — हर बार, हर shift में। Belt Conveyor एक very high-energy machine है — thousands of tonnes of coal हर घंटे move करती है, कभी-कभी 3.5 m/s की speed से। CHP एक ऐसा environment है जहाँ negligence — चाहे एक पल की ही हो — life-altering consequences दे सकती है। यह section आपको primary hazards और उनसे बचाव के तरीकों से परिचित कराता है।

text_chunks.title: 👷 Human Safety
text_chunks.content: 👷 Human Safety Entanglement in moving belt → degloving, amputation, fatality Entanglement in drive pulley nip → instant, irreversible crush injury Falling coal at transfer point → blunt trauma, fracture Belt fire → smoke inhalation, burn injuries Coal dust explosion → blast and burn injuries across large area Slipping on coal spillage → fall from height in transfer towers (potentially fatal) Electrical contact near damaged panels → electrocution Every failure in this list was, at some point, preventable . Most machinery failures begin with a small defect — a seized idler, a worn scraper, a loose guard, a misaligned belt — that was visible for days before the failure happened. The difference between a major accident and a near-miss is often one person who was paying attention and reported what they saw. As an intern, your most valuable contribution to plant safety is having the awareness to recognise and report early signs of deterioration — and this course is giving you exactly that awareness.

text_chunks.content: इस Course में आप क्या सीखोगे ✓ Boiler तक continuous fuel supply में conveyor system का role समझना। ✓ सारे major conveyor components identify करना और उनका system में क्या काम है यह समझना। ✓ Visualize करना कि coal, unloading point (wagon tippler) से boiler bunker तक कैसे travel करती है। ✓ Belt conveyor में motion, load carrying, और tension balance का mechanism समझना। ✓ यह पहचानना कि capacity limits system stability और plant performance को कैसे affect करती हैं। ✓ High-risk zones जैसे transfer points, drive pulleys, और rotating parts के बारे में awareness develop करना। ✓ Upstream systems जैसे wagon tippler, conveyor behaviour को सीधे कैसे affect करता है, यह समझना।

text_chunks.title: यह Course कैसे इस्तेमाल करें
text_chunks.content: यह Course कैसे इस्तेमाल करें यह course इसलिए बनाया गया है ताकि आप Coal Handling Plant के belt conveyor system की पूरी mental picture बना सकें — site पर जाने से पहले। सोचिए जैसे पूरा system अपने दिमाग में download कर रहे हों, ताकि जब आप physically वहाँ पहुँचें, तो हर चीज़ पहचान सकें, उसका reason समझ सकें, और यह भी जान सकें कि खतरा कहाँ है। यह सिर्फ एक context और awareness course है। इसमें यह नहीं बताया गया कि कोई भी equipment कैसे start, stop, या operate करते हैं। आप कभी भी कोई भी operational action अकेले attempt मत करना — plant management से formal training और authorization लेने के बाद ही करना। यह course complete करने के बाद आप Coal Handling Plant में walk कर सकोगे, belt conveyor system के हर major component को identify कर सकोगे, power generation में उसका role समझोगे, और — सबसे important — hazardous zones और ऐसे behaviours पहचान सकोगे जो आपको या दूसरों को injury दे सकते हैं।

text_blocks.title: Uneven Loading → Belt Drift → Structural Damage
text_blocks.content: Uneven Loading → Belt Drift → Structural Damage Cause: Coal from the feeder drops consistently to one side of the belt (e.g., feeder gate partially blocked, chute misaligned). The belt carries more load on one side than the other. What Happens: The belt gradually drifts toward the heavier side. It contacts the steel frame of the conveyor structure. Friction between the belt edge and the frame generates heat. Over hours, the belt edge begins to abrade. Coal spillage begins at the affected side. If not corrected, the belt tears longitudinally — a full-length split requiring complete belt replacement. Early Signs: Belt sway alarm activates. Visible drift at one or more idler sets. Spillage on one side only. Squealing noise from belt-structure contact. Consequence: Forced conveyor shutdown. Belt replacement cost (₹10–40 lakhs). 2–5 days of downtime for re-belting.

text_blocks.title: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment)
text_blocks.content: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment) The belt naturally tends to drift (wander sideways) if there is any asymmetry — uneven loading, idlers not perfectly perpendicular to belt travel, wind, or a bent frame. Even a slight drift accumulates over the length of the belt. If not corrected, the belt edge contacts the conveyor structure, causing edge damage, spillage, and ultimately belt failure. Self-aligning idlers and training idlers are used to correct drift automatically. A drifted belt that contacts the steel structure can generate enough heat through friction to ignite coal dust — causing a conveyor fire. Belt fires in CHP are a major risk and have caused plant outages lasting weeks.

text_blocks.title: Safety Device Reference Guide
text_blocks.content: Safety Device Reference Guide Device | Location on Conveyor | Function | Response When Activated ; Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) | Both sides, full length of conveyor, approximately every 30–50 m | Allows any person anywhere along the conveyor to immediately stop it in an emergency by pulling the rope/wire | Immediate emergency stop of conveyor drive motor. Conveyor cannot restart until EPC is reset and root cause investigated. ; Belt Sway Switch (BSW) | Both sides, spaced every 50–75 m along carry and return strand | Detects lateral drift of the belt beyond a set limit. Has two positions: first position = alarm; second position = trip. | First activation: Alarm in control room. Second (greater drift): Conveyor trip. Prevents belt edge from contacting steel structure. ; Zero Speed Switch (ZSS) | Tail pulley shaft or on a return idler | Monitors belt speed. Detects if the belt has stopped (zero speed) while the motor is still running — indicating belt slip. | Conveyor trip + alarm. Prevents drive pulley from running against a stationary belt (which causes fire from friction). ; Belt Weigher (BW) | Fixed location on the conveyor, typically mid-span | Measures the weight of coal on the belt per unit length using load cells. Calculates instantaneous TPH and cumulative tonnes. | Data sent to control room / DCS. No trip — provides operational data. High load may trigger an alarm. ; Chute Blocked Detector (CBD) | Inside transfer chutes at transfer points | Detects when coal has accumulated and blocked the chute (using vibration probe, ultrasonic, or paddle switch). | Alarm in control room. May automatically stop upstream feeder to prevent further coal accumulation. ; Thermal / Fire Detector | Inside conveyor galleries (tunnels) and transfer towers | Detects elevated temperature indicating a developing fire. Linear heat detection cable runs along the belt gallery roof. | Fire alarm. Conveyor trip. Activation of fire suppression system (CO₂ or water mist). Control room alert. ; Underspeed Switch | Drive shaft area | Detects if belt is running slower than designed speed (but not zero). Indicates overloading or drive slip developing. | Alarm → trip if underspeed persists. Allows early intervention before full slippage occurs. ; Motor Overload Relay (OLR) | Motor control centre (MCC) / switchgear panel | Monitors motor current. If the motor draws current above the rated limit for a set time (indicating overload), it trips. | Motor trip + alarm. Conveyor stops. Investigation required to identify overload cause before restart. When you walk a conveyor on site, you will see red ropes, yellow boxes, and small switches mounted on the frame at regular intervals — these are all part of this safety system. You will hear terms like "BSW trip," "ZSS alarm," or "EPC activation" on the radio constantly. Now you know exactly what each term means, what triggered it, and what the plant team needs to do in response. On some plants, under production pressure, well-meaning but incorrect actions include bypassing a belt sway switch that keeps tripping, disabling a chute blocked detector that gives "false" alarms, or tying off an EPC that was accidentally pulled. This is an extremely dangerous practice. Every safety device bypass removes one layer of protection from the system. Multiple bypasses create a condition where a fatal accident can occur without any warning. As an intern, if you are ever asked to bypass a safety device, immediately consult your supervisor. Document it. Never accept it as routine.

text_blocks.title: Glossary of CHP & Belt Conveyor Terms
text_blocks.content: Glossary of CHP & Belt Conveyor Terms On your first day on site you will hear these terms constantly. This glossary ensures you are not lost in the conversation. Term | Meaning ; Belt | The continuous rubber-fabric loop that carries coal from tail to head end. ; Belt Conveyor (BC) | The complete conveyor assembly — numbered in sequence (BC-1, BC-2, etc.) in the plant. ; Carry Strand | The top run of the belt that carries coal toward the discharge point. ; Return Strand | The lower run of the empty belt going back from head to tail. ; Head Pulley | The drive pulley at the discharge end of the conveyor. ; Tail Pulley | The non-driven pulley at the loading end. ; Idler | A free-spinning roller that supports the belt. Troughing idlers (carry) and flat idlers (return). ; Trough Angle | The angle at which wing idler rolls are tilted to form the trough (20°–45°). ; Take-up | The tensioning device — gravity, screw, or hydraulic — that keeps the belt at correct tension. ; Lagging | Rubber coating on the drive pulley surface to increase friction with the belt. ; Skirt Board | Side rubber/steel walls at the feed point that contain coal on the belt edge. ; Scraper / Cleaner | A blade pressed against the belt at the head end to remove carryback coal. ; Carryback | Fine coal that sticks to the belt after discharge and is carried back on the return strand. ; Transfer Point | Location where coal moves from one conveyor to the next via a chute. ; Chute | The steel guide structure that directs coal from one conveyor to the next at transfer points. ; Tripper Car | A movable discharge device on a conveyor above the bunker that distributes coal across bunker bays. Term | Meaning ; Bunker | Large coal storage silo above the boiler, fed by the conveyor. Buffer for continuous boiler feeding. ; Hopper | A funnel-shaped collection vessel below the wagon tippler that collects unloaded coal. ; Feeder | A device (vibrating, apron, or belt type) that controls the rate of coal feeding onto the conveyor. ; TPH | Tonnes Per Hour — the standard unit of conveyor throughput capacity. ; CHP | Coal Handling Plant — the entire system for receiving, processing, and conveying coal in a power plant. ; DCS | Distributed Control System — the central computerised control system monitoring all CHP parameters. ; MCC | Motor Control Centre — the electrical switchgear panel that starts, stops, and protects conveyor motors. ; EPC | Emergency Pull Cord — the safety rope running the full length of the conveyor for emergency stop. ; BSW | Belt Sway Switch — sensor that detects lateral belt drift and triggers alarm/trip. ; ZSS / USS | Zero Speed Switch / Underspeed Switch — detects belt slippage or stall. ; LOTO | Lockout-Tagout — energy isolation procedure before maintenance on conveyor or any equipment. ; Nip Point | The point where the belt meets a pulley — the most dangerous entanglement zone. ; Belt Drift | Lateral wandering of the belt off centre — can cause edge damage and fire. ; Tight Side | The belt strand leaving the drive pulley (carry side) — where belt tension is highest. ; Slack Side | The belt strand returning to the drive pulley — where tension is lower. ; CWP | Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis — lung disease caused by long-term coal dust inhalation ("black lung").

text_blocks.title: Belt Drift (Belt Misalignment)
text_blocks.content: Belt Drift (Belt Misalignment) Root Cause: Off-centre loading (feeder से coal belt के center में नहीं गिर रही), worn idlers, wet/sticky coal जो एक तरफ build-up कर रही हो, misaligned pulleys, या incorrect take-up tension। Effect: Belt एक तरफ रगड़ती है conveyor structure से → belt edge fraying → material spillage → structure damage → fire risk (friction से)। Detection: BSW (Belt Sway Switch) alarm; visual patrol में belt edge की position देखें। Immediate Action: Feed rate कम करें → self-aligning idlers adjust करें → loading pattern investigate करें। BSW trip के बाद investigation के बिना restart नहीं।

text_blocks.title: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour
text_blocks.content: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour A transfer point is like a controlled handover baton pass — coal must land precisely on the next belt. Any miss, blockage, or misalignment at this point disrupts the entire downstream flow. Wherever coal moves from one conveyor to the next — or from a hopper to a conveyor — there is a transfer point . These are not minor connections; they are among the most critical and most hazardous locations in the entire Coal Handling Plant. Understanding what happens at a transfer point is essential before entering the CHP. BC-1 (Upper Conveyor) Coal on BC-1 Head Pulley TRANSFER CHUTE (guides coal) ↓ Coal falls here BC-2 (Lower Conveyor) Impact Zone Coal on BC-2 ⚠ DUST ⚠ Spillage ⚠ Spillage ⚠ BLOCKAGE RISK Wet/sticky coal can block chute Coal must land centrally on BC-2 belt. Any deviation → spillage or belt drift.

text_blocks.title: System Flow Integration – Coal का पूरा सफर
text_blocks.content: System Flow Integration – Coal का पूरा सफर Coal का सफर एक relay race की तरह है — हर stage अगली stage को handoff करती है। एक भी stage fail हुई तो पूरी race रुक जाती है। Belt conveyor system अकेले काम नहीं करता — यह एक बड़े coal handling sequence का हिस्सा है। Wagon tippler से boiler तक हर step एक specific function है जो अगले step पर निर्भर करती है। यह chain समझना ज़रूरी है। ① Railway Wagon Coal loaded BOX-N wagons railway tracks पर आते हैं ⚠ Surge loading risk ② Wagon Tippler Wagon को rotate/tilt करके coal को dump करता है ⚠ High dust generation ③ Track Hopper Coal को temporarily store करता है ⚠ Overflow risk ④ Feeder Coal की rate control करके belt पर डालता है ⚠ Overfeeding risk ⑤ Belt Conveyor BC-1 Coal को aage carry ⚠ Drift, overload risk ⑥ Transfer Tower BC-1 से BC-2 पर coal ⚠ HIGHEST RISK ZONE ⑦ Belt Conveyor BC-2 Bunker तक carry ⚠ Same risks ⑧ Coal Bunker 8–12 hrs buffer storage ⚠ Overflow / starvation ⑨ Pulveriser Coal को powder बनाता है → Boiler में जाती है ✓ Electricity generation
